Pre-existence of Christ
pree-eg-ZIS-tuhns uhv KRYST
noun (Christology)
From Latin prae, before, and existere, to stand forth or be; the eternal being of the Son of God before His incarnation in time.

📖 Biblical Definition

The pre-existence of Christ is the doctrine that the Son of God was, from all eternity, before ever He took our nature in the womb of the virgin. He did not begin to be at Bethlehem; He who was born there had no beginning. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Of Himself He testified, "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58), taking upon His lips the very name of the self-existent God. He prayed for the glory which He had with the Father "before the world was" (John 17:5). The apostle declares that He "being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God" (Phil 2:6), and that "he is before all things, and by him all things consist" (Col 1:17). Thus His pre-existence is not a created or angelic priority but the eternal, necessary being of the second Person of the Godhead. Against Arianism, which makes Him a creature; against adoptionism, which makes Him a mere man exalted to sonship; and against every modern denial of His eternal deity, this dictionary confesses that the Son is true God of true God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father, by whom all things were made.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The pre-existence of Christ is His eternal being as the Son of God before His incarnation. He existed with the Father before the world was and is the Creator of all things. This truth refutes Arianism and adoptionism alike.

expand to see more

PRE-EXISTENCE OF CHRIST, noun. The eternal subsistence of the Son of God before His incarnation in the fullness of time.

It affirms that the Word was with God and was God in the beginning, having no origin and no birth in time as to His divine nature.

"Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58).

It requires us to confess Him true and eternal God, the Creator and upholder of all things.

It forbids the Arian and Socinian errors that make Christ a creature or a mere man.

📖 Key Scripture

John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

John 8:58 — "Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am."

John 17:5 — "And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was."

Col 1:17 — "And he is before all things, and by him all things consist."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The ancient Arian heresy, revived in the Watchtower and in modern unitarian and liberal theology, denies the eternal deity of the Son, reducing Him to a created or merely human figure exalted after His life.

expand to see more

Arianism, condemned at Nicaea in 325, taught that "there was when the Son was not," making Him the first and highest of creatures rather than true God. This error lives on in the Jehovah's Witnesses, who mistranslate John 1:1 as "a god," and in every unitarian scheme that denies the eternal generation of the Son. But Scripture leaves no room for it: He who is "before all things" and by whom "all things consist" cannot Himself be a thing made. The Nicene Creed rightly confesses Him "begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father."

Adoptionism, on the other side, denies the pre-existence by making Jesus a mere man whom God adopted as Son at His baptism or resurrection. Liberal and progressive theology renews this in subtler forms, speaking of Jesus as a man uniquely filled with God rather than God who became man. Against all such, the doctrine of pre-existence holds the line: the eternal Son, who had glory with the Father before the world was, condescended to take our flesh, remaining what He was while becoming what He was not.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin prae-existere, to be beforehand; resting on the Greek en arche en ho Logos of John 1:1 and the "I am" (ego eimi) of John 8:58.

expand to see more

The term joins Latin prae, before, with existere, to stand forth or be.

John 1:1 anchors it: en arche en ho Logos, "in the beginning was the Word."

The verb en (was) denotes continuous being, set against egeneto (came to be) used of created things.

In John 8:58 Christ says ego eimi, "I am," the name of God revealed at the bush (Exod 3:14).

Philippians 2:6 speaks of His being en morphe Theou, in the very form of God, before the kenosis of the incarnation.

Usage

"The pre-existence of Christ means He did not begin to be at Bethlehem but is the eternal Son."

"Arius denied the pre-existence of Christ as eternal God, and Nicaea condemned him for it."

"When the Lord said, "Before Abraham was, I am," He claimed both pre-existence and full deity."
